finalResponse:
# Market Incident Response — Cultural Misjudgement in Campaign [X], Market [Y]
## Recommendation for the Crisis Group

**Version 0.9 — draft for decision. Prepared for the crisis group, and for simultaneous release to the market leadership team in [Y]. Not for external circulation, not for the wider marketing function, and specifically not for the agency of record until §7.2 has been settled.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document assumes something the group may wish to contest before reading further: that the fastest available response is not the same thing as the best one, and that the gap between them is roughly six hours. Almost everything expensive about incidents of this kind is decided inside that window, usually by whoever is awake.

We would therefore ask two courtesies before this travels.

First, that the market managing director and the [Y] communications lead see §§4, 6 and 7 **before** the group takes a position, and have room to respond in their own terms. A response to a local cultural misjudgement that is drafted centrally and delivered to the market as a finished artefact has already repeated the error that caused the incident. Colleagues in [Y] will notice that before they notice the apology, and so, eventually, will everyone else.

Second, that §11 (legal, regulatory and platform gates) be walked with Group Legal and local counsel before any statement is published anywhere. The most common single cause of a second news cycle is a well-intentioned apology that concedes a fact local regulators had not yet established, or that reaches a distributor after it reaches their customers.

Section 3 is a diagnosis, not a formality. We would rather spend four hours on it than four months on the consequences of skipping it. If the group's judgement is that we do not have four hours, §2 lists what can be done immediately without any diagnosis at all, and none of it forecloses a later choice.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Withdraw globally and immediately; apologise locally, specifically, in language, from a named local human, within 24 hours; devolve the response to the market with a bounded and publicly conferred mandate; resist the instinct to buy reputation back with advertising; and convert the incident into a checkable structural change in who holds creative sign-off — published at 90 days whether or not anyone is still asking.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Immediate, non-negotiable | Campaign withdrawn in **all** markets, not only [Y]; paid amplification killed; scheduled social frozen network-wide; legal hold on all creative development records (§2) |
| Response posture | To be set at §4 by the crisis group, from four defined options. Our recommendation: **Posture 2 — Withdraw and Apologise** — subject to the §3 diagnosis not revealing orchestration |
| Who speaks | The **most senior [Y]-based executive**, in [local language], in local media and local channels. Not the Group CEO. Not the CMO. Not a logo on a grey square |
| Who decides | The **[Y] market MD**, under a written, bounded, time-limited mandate conferred visibly by the Group CEO (§7.1) |
| The centre's own binding | The centre may override a market decision, but must give written reasons **to the same audience that saw the decision**, and overrides are logged and reported to the board (§7.3) |
| Sequencing rule | Employees first. Then partners and trade. Then regulators. Then affected-community interlocutors. Then media. Global markets last and quietly (§6) |
| Principal risk | Not the original offence — the **second cycle**, generated by our own response. Roughly two-thirds of durable damage in comparable incidents accrues after the first apology, not before it *(judgement — §15)* |
| Restoration mechanism | Structural, checkable, and boring: local creative authority, a standing local review panel with teeth, and one long-horizon commitment in [Y] with no brand marks on it (§9) |
| What we will not do | Buy influencers, seed comments, delete criticism, litigate against critics, or publish a "learning journey" (§13) |
| Numeric failure test | If at T+30 days negative volume has not decayed to <20% of peak **and** trade partners have not reversed withdrawal decisions, the response has failed; escalate to §12.4 rather than repeating it louder |
| Investment sought | **$2.4M** immediate response envelope; **$6.8M** twelve-month restoration (illustrative, assumptions at §14.1) |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.4, sought at the crisis group session at **T+6 hours** |
| Owner | Group Chief Communications Officer accountable; **[Y] market MD executing**; incident director named within 2 hours of approval |

### 1.1 The proposition, and how confident we are in it

An audience does not forgive a brand for being sorry. It forgives a brand for becoming *predictable again* — and predictability is demonstrated by conduct over weeks, not by language in the first 24 hours. The apology's only real job is to buy the standing to be judged on conduct.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a measured finding. The evidence key at §15 marks which statements in this document are which. The group is entitled to know where we are reasoning and where we are reporting.)*

---

## 2. The first four hours — moves that require no diagnosis

These foreclose nothing. They can be executed by the incident director on standing authority and should not wait for the crisis group to convene.

| # | Action | Owner | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pull the creative from every paid channel, **every market** | Global media lead | T+1h |
| 2 | Freeze all scheduled brand social globally, including unrelated content and other brands in the house | Social ops | T+1h |
| 3 | Remove the asset from owned properties; do **not** delete audience comments, and record that we did not | Digital | T+2h |
| 4 | Legal hold: briefs, approval chains, agency correspondence, research, translations, any local objection raised and overridden | Group Legal | T+2h |
| 5 | Holding line, one paragraph, published in [local language] first: *we have withdrawn it, we are listening, a fuller response follows within 24 hours from [named person]* | [Y] comms lead | T+3h |
| 6 | Brief customer-facing and retail staff in [Y] **before** any public statement — script, permission to acknowledge, escalation route, and explicit safety guidance | [Y] HR + ops | T+3h |
| 7 | Notify the top trade partners and distributors in [Y] by phone, not email | [Y] commercial lead | T+4h |
| 8 | Stand up listening: local-language monitoring, not English-language monitoring of a non-English market | Insight | T+2h |
| 9 | Freeze all campaign work in the region pending §9.2 | Regional CMO | T+4h |

**Note on #5.** The holding line commits to a time and a named person. That is deliberate. A holding statement that commits to nothing reads as a legal artefact and is treated as one.

**Note on #3.** Comment deletion is recoverable in exactly no cases and has ended several careers that the original creative would not have. We would ask that this be stated to the digital team as an instruction rather than a preference.

---

## 3. Diagnosis before design — four hours, run in parallel with §2

We would gently ask the group to test one framing before adopting it. The incident is currently described as *a cultural misunderstanding*. The evidence available to us may instead describe **a governance failure wearing cultural clothing** — and only one of those is fixed by an apology.

### 3.1 The three questions that change the response

**Q1 — Was there local objection, and was it overridden?**
Check the approval chain now, before anyone tidies it. If someone in [Y] flagged this and was overruled by the centre or by the agency, the story is no longer about a joke. It is about a company that does not listen to its own people, which is a considerably more durable and more damaging narrative — and one that will surface, because the person who raised the flag has a phone.

*If the answer is yes:* the apology must acknowledge the override without naming or exposing the individual, and §9.3 (structural remedy) moves from Month 3 to Week 2. Attempting to conceal it is the single highest-cost option available.

**Q2 — Who is actually offended, and in what proportion?**
Three distinguishable populations, easily conflated in a monitoring dashboard:

| Population | Signal | Response weight |
|---|---|---|
| Directly affected community in [Y] | Local-language, local platforms, community and religious/civic institutions, non-national-media | **Decisive** |
| Broadly sympathetic domestic public | Mainstream local media, general social | High |
| International commentary and diaspora | English-language, high volume, low local purchase | Moderate — real, but do not let it set the terms |
| Orchestrated or opportunistic actors | Coordinated timing, template language, competitor adjacency, political utility | See §4.3 |

The failure to separate these produces apologies pitched at the wrong audience — typically at international Twitter, in English, which reads in [Y] as further evidence that the market is an afterthought.

**Q3 — What exactly was the offence?**
Not "it was insensitive." Specifically: was it sacred/religious, ethnic or racial, historical or national-dignity, gender or family-role, class or caste, linguistic (a translation or transliteration error), or a matter of ritual propriety? These have materially different half-lives and materially different remedies. A translation error is repairable in a week; a perceived slight to national dignity can run for years and can attract state interest.

Have a local cultural interlocutor **outside the company** — not the agency, not an employee — describe the offence back to us in their own words within four hours. Then use *their* framing in the apology, not ours. This is the cheapest and most frequently skipped step in the entire response.

### 3.2 Severity classification

| Tier | Markers | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Local social irritation, no trade or regulator movement, decaying | Local correction, no global posture |
| 2 | National media, trade partners asking questions, government commentary absent | Posture 2, market-led (**most likely current state**) |
| 3 | Regulator or ministry engaged, retail delisting, boycott with an organised host, employee safety concerns | Posture 2 plus §12.4 escalation; Group CEO enters |
| 4 | Legal jeopardy, physical risk to staff, licence-to-operate threat | Separate protocol; this document is insufficient |

---

## 4. The calibration decision — four postures

We would ask the group to choose explicitly rather than to drift into one. Drift produces Posture 3 delivered with Posture 2 timing, which satisfies nobody.

| | Posture | When it fits | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Correct and continue** — fix the asset, brief note, no apology | Narrow technical error (mistranslation, wrong image credit), no dignity dimension, Tier 1 | Cheap. Fails badly if severity is misread |
| **2** | **Withdraw and apologise** — full withdrawal, unqualified apology, named accountability, structural remedy | Genuine offence to a real constituency, Tier 2–3. **Recommended** | High short-term visibility, lowest long-term cost |
| **3** | **Acknowledge and explain** — regret expressed, intent explained, asset withdrawn | Almost never. Explanation of intent reads universally as excuse | Usually generates the second cycle it seeks to avoid |
| **4** | **Hold** — withdraw quietly, decline to apologise | Genuine ambiguity **and** evidence of orchestration for commercial or political ends where concession invites escalation | High risk, occasionally correct, requires the group to accept a bad month deliberately |

### 4.1 Why we recommend Posture 2

The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and a mild internal embarrassment. An under-apology to a genuinely offended one costs a market position, and the second attempt is never believed. Given that asymmetry, we would apologise on the balance of probability rather than on proof.

### 4.2 The hedge to avoid at all costs

*"We are sorry if anyone was offended"* transfers the fault to the audience's sensitivity, is recognised as doing so in every language we are aware of, and has independently generated more coverage than the original creative in numerous comparable incidents *(judgement, though the pattern is well attested — §15)*. So has *"that was not our intent."* Intent is the brand's private property and no one else's concern. See §5.2.

### 4.3 The one circumstance in which we would counsel the group to hold its nerve

If the §3.1 Q2 analysis shows the reaction is substantially manufactured — coordinated timing, template language, a competitor or political actor with a clear interest, and **no independently locatable community objection** — then a full apology rewards the mechanism and reliably invites a repeat within the year.

We flag this not because we believe it is the current case (we do not, on present evidence), but because we would rather the group considered and rejected it in the next four hours than discovered it in six weeks. The test is falsifiable and cheap: can we find, in four hours, three credible local community or civic voices, unconnected to each other and to the campaign, who articulate the offence in their own terms? If yes, Posture 2, without further debate. If no, bring it back to the group before publishing.

---

## 5. The apology — architecture, not wording

Wording is the market's property (§7.1). Architecture is what we would ask to be fixed.

### 5.1 Eight components

| # | Component | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Name the offence in the offended community's own terms** | Taken from §3.1 Q3. Using their framing is the entire signal |
| 2 | **Unconditional regret** | No "if", no "any", no "may have" |
| 3 | **Named human accountability** | A senior [Y]-based person, by name and face. Corporate voice is the voice of an entity avoiding a person |
| 4 | **What has already been done** | Past tense, verifiable, ideally completed before publishing |
| 5 | **What will change in how decisions are made** | The only forward-looking element that carries weight |
| 6 | **A date** | A public commitment to report back at 90 days |
| 7 | **A route to be answered** | A monitored channel, in language, with a response commitment |
| 8 | **Nothing else** | No product mention. No values statement. No history of our community contribution. Each addition dilutes the whole |

### 5.2 The prohibited constructions

| Phrase pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "…if anyone was offended" | Conditional; blames the audience |
| "…was not our intention" | Irrelevant; heard as excuse |
| "…does not reflect who we are" | It does; it was approved by people who work here |
| "We have always celebrated diversity…" | Invites the receipts |
| "…a learning journey" | Frames harm as our development opportunity |
| "…the actions of an individual" | Scapegoating; sequel guaranteed |
| Passive voice for the offence, active voice for the remedy | Universally noticed |

### 5.3 Form and channel

Local language first and natively written — **not translated from an English original**, which is detectable and, in this specific context, itself part of the offence. Local platforms in [Y] before global platforms. Video is warmer than text and harder to quote out of context; a plain, unproduced, single-take piece to camera outperforms a produced statement *(judgement)*. No music. No brand furniture. No grey square.

**Timing:** within 24 hours of the incident being recognised, and not on a Friday evening local time, which is read everywhere as burial.

---

## 6. Sequencing — who hears it, in what order

Almost every avoidable injury in the next fortnight is a sequencing failure rather than a content failure.

| Order | Audience | Channel | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Y] employees, especially customer-facing and retail | Manager cascade, in person or by voice, with a script and permission to acknowledge | Before anything public |
| 2 | Employees globally | Internal note, brief, honest, no spin | T+6h |
| 3 | Trade partners, distributors, key retail accounts in [Y] | Named-person phone calls | T+8h |
| 4 | Regulators, relevant ministries, industry bodies in [Y] | Local counsel and government affairs, in the local convention | Before media |
| 5 | Affected-community interlocutors | Private, listening posture, **no cameras, no request for absolution** | T+12–24h |
| 6 | [Y] media and public | Statement per §5 | T+24h |
| 7 | International media | Reactive only. Point them to the local statement | On enquiry |
| 8 | Other markets | Quiet brief to market leads; no proactive global publication | T+36h |

**On #5.** The single most common error is to meet community representatives and photograph it. The meeting has value; the photograph converts it into a transaction and reliably offends the people it was intended to reassure. If a record is wanted, let the community party decide whether and how to describe it.

**On #8.** We would suggest the group resist the instinct to publish a global apology. In markets where the incident has not landed, a global statement creates the awareness it seeks to manage, and the coverage will be about the apology rather than about anything else. Contain the response geographically to the extent that platform reality permits, and be honest that it permits less than it used to.

---

## 7. Authority — who decides, and what the centre binds itself to

### 7.1 The market mandate

We recommend that the Group CEO confer, in writing and visibly, a **bounded mandate** on the [Y] market MD:

> *For the next 30 days, [name] decides the content, timing, language and channel of all communications relating to this incident in [Y], and the composition of the local remedy up to a value of $[1.5]M. They do not need to ask. Escalation to the crisis group is required only for the four reserved matters below. If you disagree with a decision they have taken, take it to them.*

**Reserved to the centre (four only):** legal admissions with cross
